original_question: Let gamma be a closed strictly convex hypersurface in R^n, let Pi be the phase cylinder of oriented lines intersecting gamma transversally at two points, fix epsilon > 0 and k in N, and consider a C-infinity Hamiltonian symplectomorphism Pi -> Pi. Is every such symplectomorphism a C-infinity limit of compositions of reflections from gamma and from hypersurfaces that are epsilon-close to gamma in the C^k topology, using reflections only and not inverses?
target_in_paper: Alexey Glutsyuk, Problem 2, specifically the displayed Question [14, Sect. 1.6] about approximating Hamiltonian symplectomorphisms of the phase cylinder by compositions of reflections, read together with the immediately following remark explaining that the unresolved point is to use reflections without inverses. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches almost everything in the paper's displayed question: the ambient space R^n, a closed strictly convex hypersurface γ, the phase cylinder of oriented lines meeting γ transversally in two points, fixed ε > 0 and k in N, a C^∞-smooth Hamiltonian symplectomorphism Π -> Π, C^∞ approximation by compositions of reflections from γ and from hypersurfaces ε-close to γ in the C^k topology, and the crucial 'reflections only, no inverses' emphasis supplied by the following remark. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
missing_details: The paper ties Π specifically to the billiard inside the domain bounded by γ; that bounded-domain context should be stated explicitly. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

Π is not just any line space: it is an open subset of the space of oriented lines in R^n, equipped with the standard symplectic structure. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

To make the question stand-alone, Π should be defined explicitly rather than only named as the 'phase cylinder.' ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The approximation is in the C^∞ topology on maps Π -> Π; saying only 'C^∞ limit' leaves that topology implicit. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The approximants are finite compositions of reflections from γ and from hypersurfaces ε-close to γ in the C^k topology; 'finite compositions' is implicit but worth making explicit. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))

The 'without inverses' clause is not part of the displayed question itself; it comes from the immediately following remark, which says the version allowing reflections and their inverses was proved in [14]. A paper-faithful stand-alone version should therefore mention that this is the remaining unsolved restriction. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
refined_question: Let γ ⊂ R^n be a closed strictly convex hypersurface, and let Π be the phase cylinder for the billiard in the domain bounded by γ, i.e. the open subset of the space of oriented lines in R^n consisting of those lines that intersect γ transversally at two points, equipped with its standard symplectic structure. Fix ε > 0 and k in N. Is every C^∞-smooth Hamiltonian symplectomorphism Φ: Π -> Π a C^∞ limit of finite compositions of reflections from γ and from hypersurfaces that are ε-close to γ in the C^k topology, with no inverses of reflections allowed? ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
justification: This is the nearest official formulation in arXiv:2110.10750: in Alexey Glutsyuk's Problem 2, the paper defines the phase cylinder Π for a closed strictly convex hypersurface γ and then asks essentially your question verbatim. The only extra ingredient in your draft, namely 'using reflections only and not inverses,' is exactly the point stressed in the following remark: the paper states that the positive answer was already proved in [14] when inverses of reflections are also allowed, and concludes that the important remaining issue is to understand limits of compositions of reflections without inverses. I therefore kept the scope global and strictly convex, avoided drifting to the local/germ and Riemannian variants discussed in [14], and only added the setup needed to make the question self-contained. ([armj.math.stonybrook.edu](https://armj.math.stonybrook.edu/pdf-Springer-final/022-0198.pdf))
